newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Kremlin slams report on return of Tsar's heir.
newsitem.headline: Kremlin slams report on return of Tsar's heir.

text.p: The Kremlin on Monday poured scorn on a report that President Boris Yeltsin was planning to welcome home a 15-year-old claimant to Russia's imperial throne.

The London Daily Telegraph, quoting an unidentified Kremlin source, said last week that Grand Duke Georgy Mikhailovich Romanov would be reinstated as the head of Russia's imperial family in the near future.
Kremlin spokesman Sergei Yastrzhembsky said the report, picked up by other British and Russian media, was "not serious".

"It would be funny if it wasn't annoying," Yastrzhembsky told a news briefing. "One has the impression that the British mass media has run out of its own monarchy stories and they want to expand -- including into Russian territory."

"I would recommend that you pay attention to more serious problems which unfortunately we have more than enough of. I would not pay attention to such tricks and mind games of people who are far from Russia," he said.
The surviving members of the Romanov dynasty have been living in exile since 1918 when the Bolsheviks massacred the last tsar, Nicholas II, and his family following the Russian revolution.

The Telegraph report said Grand Duke Georgy would be accompanied by his mother and grandmother and would live in the village of Maloye Kolchugino -- a former dacha complex for politburo members near Moscow.
A former senior bodyguard to Yeltsin would be tutor to Georgy, who would enter the Suvorovsky military academy in Moscow, it said.

The report said that their role would be merely ceremonial and that the plan to bring them back was part of a Kremlin programme called the Russian National Idea, which aims to restore lost Russian pride and culture.

Alexander Klimov of the Monarchist Movement of Russia said that he thought the report was a trial balloon but stressed his view that if a successor was brought back it would be another claimant, Prince Nicholas Romanov who lives in Switzerland.

But he added that a presidential decree could play no role in the return of the royal family. "Yeltsin has no right to issue any decrees on this matter because Russia is not the direct inheritor of the Russian empire," he said.
"It can be done only by the free will of the people," he added, but declined to say how such a process would work.
The monarchist movement has little popular support in Russia and is divided by the competing claims of various successors.
There is no direct heir to the Russian throne and in the past a gathering of Russian nobility nominated a future tsar in similar situations. The choice had to be approved by the Orthodox Church.
